content.title: Dos paquetes y una etiqueta
content.story:
Cuando Elena entró en la tienda, el dueño estaba colocando dos paquetes sobre el mostrador. Ambos eran pequeños y estaban envueltos en papel marrón.

—Buenos días. Vengo a buscar mi paquete —dijo Elena—. Me llamaron esta mañana.

—Claro, aquí lo tiene —respondió Tomás, el dueño.

Elena tomó el paquete que él le ofrecía, pero al leer la etiqueta, frunció el ceño.

—Este no me pertenece. Aquí dice «Tomás Ruiz».

—Sí, soy yo —contestó él—. Mi nombre aparece porque recibí el paquete.

Elena lo miró, todavía con el paquete en las manos.

—Pero yo esperaba unos libros. Esto pesa muy poco.

Tomás señaló el otro paquete.

—Entonces debe ser ese. Creía que el más pesado era el café que pedí para mí.

Elena dejó el primero sobre el mostrador. Tomás acercó el segundo y los dos leyeron la etiqueta: «Elena Vargas». Debajo aparecía la dirección de la tienda.

—Este sí es mío —dijo ella—. Pedí que lo enviaran aquí porque durante el día no estoy en casa.

Tomás volvió a mirar el paquete que llevaba su nombre. En una esquina había un dibujo de una taza.

—Ahora lo entiendo. Este me pertenece a mí. Confundí los paquetes porque tenían el mismo papel y no leí bien las etiquetas.

Elena sonrió.

—Por suerte, no abrimos ninguno.

Después de aclarar la confusión, Tomás le entregó el paquete de los libros. Elena lo guardó en su bolsa y se dispuso a salir, pero entonces vio un sobre en el suelo, junto al mostrador.

—¿Esto también venía con mi paquete?

Tomás se agachó para recogerlo.

—No lo sé. Vamos a ver a quién pertenece.

glossary.meaning: Parcel or package.
Label; here, it shows the recipient's name.
To belong to someone. With me, the owner is the speaker.
To mix up or mistake one thing for another.
To clear up or explain.
To believe or think that. Creía introduces Tomás's earlier mistaken assumption.
Shop counter.
To frown, often because of confusion or concern.
To get ready to do something.
The imperfect sets the background or describes expectations; the preterite presents completed actions that move the scene forward.

content.title: Dos paquetes y una etiqueta
content.story:
Cuando Clara entró en la tienda, llovía y había varias personas esperando. Detrás del mostrador, el dueño, Ramón, buscaba algo en un cajón. A su lado había dos paquetes envueltos en papel marrón: uno grande y otro pequeño.

—Buenas tardes. Vengo a buscar mi paquete —dijo Clara—. Me llamaron esta mañana.

—Sí, un momento —respondió Ramón.

El teléfono empezó a sonar. Ramón señaló el paquete grande mientras levantaba el teléfono.

—Ese es el suyo.

Clara lo tomó con cuidado. Pesaba mucho más de lo que esperaba. Ella había dejado una lámpara pequeña en la tienda para que Ramón la reparara, pero creyó que él había usado una caja grande para protegerla.

Cuando Ramón terminó la llamada, Clara ya estaba junto a la puerta.

—¡Espere! —dijo él—. ¿Adónde lleva mi paquete?

Clara se volvió, sorprendida.

—A mi casa. Usted me dijo que era mío.

—Creí que venía a recogerlo para la empresa de transporte. Ese paquete me pertenece. Son libros que voy a enviar a mi hermano.

Clara regresó al mostrador y dejó la caja grande sobre él.

—Yo soy Clara Medina. Vine por mi lámpara.

Ramón miró el paquete pequeño.

—Entonces este debe ser el suyo. Pero aquí dice «Ramón».

Los dos se quedaron mirando la etiqueta pegada al papel.

—¿Puedo verla? —preguntó Clara.

Ramón giró el paquete. Debajo de su nombre había otras palabras, escritas con una letra más pequeña: «Por favor, revisar el cable. Clara Medina».

Clara se rio.

—La nota era para usted. Puse su nombre arriba para que supieran quién tenía que reparar la lámpara.

Ramón se dio cuenta de que había confundido el nombre de la persona que debía recibir la nota con el de la dueña del paquete.

—Ahora está claro —dijo—. Y yo señalé la caja grande porque esperaba al conductor de la empresa de transporte.

Abrió el paquete pequeño para comprobar su contenido. Dentro estaba la lámpara azul de Clara, con el cable nuevo. La conectó y la luz se encendió.

—Esta sí es mía —dijo ella.

Ramón volvió a envolverla y escribió «Clara Medina» en una etiqueta nueva. En la caja grande puso el nombre y la dirección de su hermano.

Clara guardó su paquete en una bolsa. Ya no llovía tanto, así que decidió salir antes de que empeorara el tiempo.

En ese momento entró un hombre con una chaqueta mojada.

—Buenas tardes. Vengo por un paquete de Ramón.

Ramón y Clara se miraron y sonrieron.

—Antes de llevarse nada —dijo Ramón al hombre—, vamos a comprobar la dirección.

glossary.meaning: When; introduces the time at which something happened.
To enter or come in; entró describes a completed past action.
Shop or store.
To rain; llovía describes the ongoing weather in the past.
There was or there were; había describes what was present in the scene.
Several; varias agrees with the feminine plural personas.
Person; personas is plural.
To wait for someone; esperando describes people waiting, and esperaba describes the shopkeeper waiting for the driver.
Behind; del combines de and el.
Shop counter.
Owner; dueño refers to the shop's male owner, while dueña refers to the parcel's female owner.
To look for or collect something; buscaba describes an ongoing search, while buscar refers to collecting the parcel.
Something.
Drawer.
Beside him; su refers to the shopkeeper here.
Two.
Parcel or package; paquetes is plural.
Wrapped; envueltos agrees with the masculine plural paquetes.
Paper used to wrap the parcels.
Brown; describes the wrapping paper.
One; stands for one of the two parcels.
The other; refers to the second parcel.
Large or big; describes the parcel and box.
Small; pequeño describes the parcel, and pequeña describes the lamp or handwriting.
Good afternoon; a polite greeting.
To come; Vengo is present tense, venía describes an assumed past purpose, and Vine is a completed past action.
My; placed before a noun to show possession.
To say or tell; dijo is a completed past action, and dice is present tense used for what the label says.
To call someone by telephone; llamaron is a completed past action with an unstated plural subject.
This morning.
Yes; also emphasizes that this really is her lamp in Esta sí es mía.
One moment; a request to wait briefly.
To reply or answer; respondió is a completed past action.
Telephone.
To start doing something; empezó a sonar means the telephone started ringing.
To ring; describes the telephone's sound.
To point to or indicate; señaló and señalé are completed past forms for he and I.
While; connects actions happening at the same time.
To lift or pick up; levantaba describes picking up the telephone.
That one or that; identifies the large parcel or a particular moment.
To be; es and soy are present forms, era gives past background, and Son identifies the contents as books.
Yours; a masculine singular possessive expression referring to the parcel and addressing someone formally.
It; a masculine direct-object pronoun referring to the large parcel.
To take or pick up; tomó describes Clara taking the parcel.
Carefully; without rough handling.
To weigh or be heavy; Pesaba describes the parcel's weight in the past.
Much more than; introduces a comparison with what someone expected.
forms: mucho más de lo que esperaba

glossary.meaning: To expect; esperaba describes Clara's expectation of the parcel's weight.
She; refers to Clara.
To leave something somewhere or put it down; había dejado means had left, while dejó is a completed past action.
Lamp.
So that; introduces a purpose and is followed here by past subjunctive forms.
To repair or fix; reparara is past subjunctive after para que, while reparar is the infinitive.
But; introduces a contrast.
To believe or think; creyó and Creí describe what Clara and Ramón mistakenly thought.
He or him; the accent distinguishes this pronoun from the article el.
To use; había usado means had used, before Clara formed her belief.
Box.
To protect; protegerla means to protect it, with la referring to the lamp.
To finish; terminó describes the completed end of the call.
Telephone call.
Already; shows that Clara was by the door when the call ended.
To be in a place or state; estaba is past background, and está describes the present situation.
Next to or beside.
Door.
To wait or stop briefly; Espere is a polite command addressed with usted.
Where to; asks about a destination.
To take or carry something to a place; lleva is a present form addressed to usted.
To turn around; se volvió describes Clara turning back.
Surprised; sorprendida agrees with Clara.
Home; A mi casa means to my home.
You, in polite or formal address; it takes third-person verb forms.
Me or to me; used when Clara is called or told something and when Ramón says the parcel belongs to him.
Mine; mío agrees with the masculine parcel, and mía agrees with the feminine lamp.
To collect or pick up; recogerlo includes lo, referring to the parcel.
Company or business.
Transport or delivery; the company moves parcels.
To belong; me pertenece means it belongs to me.
Book; libros is plural.
To be going to do something; voy a enviar expresses an intention, and vamos a comprobar proposes the next action.
To send.
Brother.
To return or go back; regresó describes Clara returning to the counter.
On or on top of; indicates where Clara puts the box.
I; explicitly naming the speaker adds emphasis here.
To come for or to collect something.
To look at; miró is a completed action, and mirando describes continued looking.
Then or in that case; introduces a conclusion.
This one; refers to the small parcel.
Must or should; debe expresses a likely conclusion, while debía describes who was supposed to receive the note.
Here; refers to the writing on the label.
Both of them; refers to Clara and Ramón together.
To keep looking or remain looking at something; describes both people examining the label.
Label attached to a parcel.
Stuck or attached; pegada agrees with the feminine etiqueta.
Can or may; Puedo asks permission to see the label.
To see or look at; verla includes la, referring to the label.
To ask a question; preguntó is a completed past action.
To turn or rotate; giró describes turning the parcel to show the writing.
Under or below.
His, her, or your in formal address; the owner is understood from the context.
Name.
Word; palabras is plural.
Other or additional; otras agrees with the feminine plural palabras.
Written; escritas agrees with the feminine plural palabras.
Handwriting or lettering; here it refers to the size of the written words.
More; makes pequeña comparative: smaller.
Please; makes the request polite.
To check or inspect; the infinitive is used as a written instruction.
Electrical cord or cable of the lamp.
To laugh; se rio describes a completed past action.
Written note or message.
For; identifies the intended recipient of the note or parcel.
To put or write something in a place; Puse and puso are completed past forms for I and he.
At the top; describes the position of Ramón's name on the note.
To know; supieran is past subjunctive after para que, expressing the intended result.
Who; identifies the person responsible for repairing the lamp.
To have to; tenía que expresses a past responsibility.
To realize that; se dio cuenta de que introduces Ramón's discovery.
To mix up or mistake one thing for another; había confundido means had mixed up.
To receive; refers to the intended recipient of the note.
Now; contrasts the resolved situation with the earlier misunderstanding.
To be clear or understood.
Because; introduces the reason for Ramón's action.
Driver; here, the delivery company's driver.
To open; Abrió is a completed past action.
To check or verify; used for checking the parcel's contents and the delivery address.
Contents; what is inside the parcel.
Inside.
Blue; describes Clara's lamp.
New; nuevo describes the cable, and nueva describes the label.
To plug in or connect electrically; conectó describes plugging in the lamp.
It; a feminine direct-object pronoun referring to the lamp in La conectó.
Light; here, the light produced by the lamp.
To turn on or light up; se encendió describes the light coming on.
This one; feminine because it refers to the lamp.
To do something again; volvió a envolverla means he wrapped it again.
To wrap; envolverla includes la, referring to the lamp.
To write; escribió is a completed past action.
Address; the destination written on the parcel.
To put away or store; guardó describes putting the parcel into a bag.
Bag.
No longer; indicates that the earlier situation has changed.
So much; describes the amount of rain.
So or therefore; introduces a consequence.
To decide; decidió is a completed past action.
To leave or go out.
Before something happens; followed here by the past subjunctive empeorara.
To get worse; empeorara refers to a possible worsening of the weather.
Weather; here, the rainy conditions outside.
At that moment.
Man.
Jacket.
Wet; mojada agrees with the feminine chaqueta.
To look at each other; se miraron describes a mutual glance.
To smile; sonrieron is a completed past action with a plural subject.
Before doing something; followed by an infinitive.
To take something away with oneself.
Anything in this context: before taking anything away.

materialIssues: “Pedí que lo enviaran aquí” combines a past request, imperfect subjunctive and object pronoun. This is a noticeable step beyond the guide's straightforward past narration and needs contextual grammatical support.

“Mi nombre aparece porque recibí el paquete” offers an initially plausible explanation, but the story never explicitly distinguishes this assumption from Tomás's later realization that the parcel is his own order.
strengths: Connected narration uses past forms, agreement and references consistently.
The notes accurately explain the selected contextual meanings, including the emphatic ownership expression and background/action contrast.
The unidentified envelope supplies a concrete, natural unresolved thread.

materialIssues: “Ella había dejado una lámpara pequeña en la tienda para que Ramón la reparara, pero creyó que él había usado una caja grande para protegerla” combines two pluperfect clauses, a purpose clause with imperfect subjunctive, reported belief and attached object pronouns. The cumulative processing load exceeds the guide's preference for straightforward subordinate clauses, despite useful notes.

“Puse su nombre arriba para que supieran quién tenía que reparar la lámpara” nests an indirect question inside a subjunctive purpose clause. The unstated plural subject of “supieran” also introduces unspecified people without establishing who they are.

“Ramón se dio cuenta de que había confundido el nombre de la persona que debía recibir la nota con el de la dueña del paquete” layers a realization clause, pluperfect, relative clause and noun ellipsis in “el de”. This is substantially denser than the surrounding B1-oriented narration.

strengths: The glossary provides broad, context-sensitive support, including common words, agreement, pronoun references and demanding verb forms.
Separate entries for “esperar” correctly distinguish waiting, expecting and the polite command; they are not merely redundant notes.
The interruption, mistaken collection purpose and misleading repair note establish clear causes for the misunderstanding.
The arriving collector continues the parcel theme and leaves address verification pending, although this hook is less substantial than sample-1's unidentified envelope.
